The soundbox is a rectangular wooden structure, usually of a solid local wood such as teak or rosewood. On top of the body are carefully hammered flat metal plates of brass or another alloy, which keep the tone clear and carrying. The beaters are bamboo sticks with padded ends, the padding usually wound from cotton or hemp cloth to give a warm timbre. The whole design combines the resonance of wood with the brightness of metal.
泰國小金屬琴的音色清晰而富有穿透力，具有明亮、溫潤的金屬質感，帶有輕盈的樂音韻味: The small Thai metallophone has a clear, penetrating timbre, a bright and warm metallic quality, and a light, musical ring. Its range lies in the upper middle register, its notes are clear and separate, and the scale is well defined. Its resonance is particular because of the rectangular wooden soundbox beneath, which amplifies and lengthens the after-ring of each note so that the sound is resonant and continuous. Compared with the low, heavy marimba, it is lighter and more transparent; compared with the vibraphone, its tone is firmer and has no tremolo. Altogether the instrument sounds elegant and refined, with both the gloss of a metal instrument and the warmth given by a wooden soundbox.

It is built of flat metal bars laid over a rectangular wooden soundbox, and is played by striking the bars with two bamboo mallets with soft heads. The instrument is similar in construction and playing to the neighbouring Khmer roneat dek, which shows how musical cultures influenced and exchanged with one another in Southeast Asia. The Thai metallophone came to be widely used in court music and in folk bands, and it has become an inseparable part of Thai traditional music.

It appeared during the reign of King Rama IV (1854-1868), reflecting the demands of Thai musical art at the time. The metallophone consists of flat metal plates set over a rectangular wooden soundbox and is played with bamboo sticks with padded ends, producing a clear, pleasing tone.
